Prevention: Plough soil to destroy pupae and weeds
Control grassy weeds in the field which can act as host plant
Nitrogen fertilizer according to recommended rates (don’t over fertilize
Conserve natural enemies such as parasitic wasps, predatory beetles, spiders, dragonflies, and predatory crickets by reducing pesticide sprays and planting flowering plants along bunds
Monitoring: Larval damage as cutting off leaves and panicles on upper portion of the rice canopy on cloudy days or at night
The adult feeds, mates and migrates at night, and rests in daytime at the base of the plant
In dry-land fields, armyworm pupate in the soil or at the base of rice plants.
In wetlands, they pupate on the plants or on grassy areas along the field borders
Scout field once a week from tillering to flowering
Use sweep net to monitor moths
If infestations of the flag leaves are high (> 50%) during maximum tillering and maturity stage, consider applying direct control
Direct Control: Place ashes in the trenches to make it more difficult for the caterpillars to escape
Place branches around fields to give armyworms a place to congregate where they can be easily collected by hand
Avoid killing natural enemies of armyworms such as wasps and spiders
Use sweep net to catch and destroy moths
Use botanical pesticides (e.g. neem, tobacco, chili)
Insecticides should be the last resort for armyworm control
Restrictions: Spray in morning between 6-10 am or in afternoon between 3-6 pm
Killing natural enemies could lead to outbreaks of secondary pests like brown plant hopper
Organo phosphate; IRAC Group 1B; WHO Class
